title: The Weather of Milton Flats
premise: Beatrix Nystrom has spent fifteen years writing postcards to her brother Elias at an address that burned down in the fire that fractured the Nystrom family—postcards she never sends, practicing the confession she cannot speak. When a stranger named Daniel Okafor appears at their mother's funeral calling the family by their true surname, Nyström-Voss, he forces open the question everyone arranged their lives around: what really happened the night of the fire, and where is Elias? As Beatrix and Daniel, bound by a shared secret neither fully understands, excavate the town's complicity, they discover Elias is alive, imprisoned for a crime Beatrix committed, and dying. In the end, Beatrix chooses truth over the loyalty that protected her, confessing publicly to save him—trading her invisibility for a justice the law can no longer touch.
about_author: Jude Sandoval is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper obituary writer who spent a decade collecting the stories families tell and the ones they don't. This is their second novel, written in a rented farmhouse where the mail still arrives for people who moved away years ago.

chapters.title: The Undeliverable
chapters.summary: Beatrix, first-person POV, writes her weekly postcard to Elias at the burned address, revealing her ritual of almost-confession. She prepares for her mother's funeral with the practiced numbness of a woman who has rehearsed grief for fifteen years. Emotional beat: the ache of disciplined silence.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Grave
chapters.summary: At the funeral, a man named Daniel Okafor appears, and Beatrix overhears him call her family by the name nobody uses—Nyström-Voss. Her brother Anders confronts him; Daniel claims to be a friend of Elias. Beatrix's POV; the beat is a crack opening in fifteen years of plaster.

chapters.title: What the Family Arranged
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV: he watches the Nystrom siblings perform unity at the reception—Anders the loyal son, sister Maren the deflector, Beatrix the ghost. He knows things about Elias he isn't saying yet. Emotional beat: the stranger as mirror, seeing what the family cannot.

chapters.title: The House That Didn't Burn
chapters.summary: Beatrix gives Daniel a ride to the old property out of obligation. Walking the scorched lot, he asks a question too precise to be innocent: who started the fire? Beatrix deflects, but her hands shake. Her POV; the beat is terror disguised as hospitality.

chapters.title: Postcards, Unsent
chapters.summary: Daniel, having glimpsed Beatrix's postcard box, begins investigating the fire through old newspaper archives. He learns Elias was declared dead without a body. His POV; the beat is the thrill and guilt of digging where grief has paved everything over.

chapters.title: Maren's Version
chapters.summary: Maren, POV chapter, tells Beatrix the family story as rehearsed: Elias ran off, the fire was an accident, the name change was for a fresh start. But Maren's version has a seam in it—she mentions a night Beatrix was supposedly away. The beat: loyalty as a story told in unison.

chapters.title: The Question Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Beatrix, alone, retrieves a hidden letter from Elias—the last thing he ever wrote her, half-burned, saying he knew what she did. She nearly burns it; she can't. Her POV; the beat is the weight of evidence she has carried like a stone in her chest.

chapters.title: Daniel's Debt
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV: we learn why he came—he owes Elias his life from a shared past Daniel has never explained to anyone, and Elias asked him, before disappearing, to check on the family 'when the last of them lets go.' The funeral was the signal. The beat: duty arriving as an inheritance.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Daniel, drawn together by mutual suspicion turning to recognition, share a night of near-confessions on her porch. She tells him about the postcards; he tells her almost everything else. Her POV; the beat is love arriving sideways, through the truth they circle.

chapters.title: Anders Draws a Line
chapters.summary: Anders, POV, warns Daniel to leave town, revealing he knows more than he admits—he was the one who drove Elias to the bus station, or so he says. His loyalty to the family story is fierce and frightened. The beat: the enforcer who is also a prisoner.

chapters.title: The Fire Marshal's File
chapters.summary: Daniel obtains the old investigation file: the fire was ruled arson, and the prime suspect was Elias, who vanished the same week. The evidence was thin; someone pushed the case closed fast. His POV; the beat is the machinery of a buried injustice clicking into view.

chapters.title: What Beatrix Did
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, the novel's hinge: a full flashback to the night of the fire. She set it—to destroy her father's ledgers documenting his crimes—and Elias took the blame and ran so she could stay free. The beat: the confession the reader has earned, delivered in her voice at last.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Daniel confronts Beatrix with the file. She tells him the truth about the fire and about Elias. His reaction is not judgment but relief—he finally knows why Elias carried himself like a man serving a sentence. Alternating close third; the beat is two people setting down the same weight.

chapters.title: Where the Postcards Go
chapters.summary: Daniel reveals what he has withheld: Elias is alive, imprisoned under a different name in another state, and he is sick. The postcards Beatrix wrote for fifteen years were never undeliverable—Elias received them through Daniel, all along. Her POV; the beat is devastation and hope in the same breath.

chapters.title: Maren Breaks
chapters.summary: Maren, POV, learns the truth from Beatrix and shatters—not with anger but with grief for the years the family's arrangement cost everyone. She reveals the final piece: their father knew Beatrix did it and used it to control them all until his death. The beat: the loyal daughter choosing her sister over the story.

chapters.title: The Family Arrangement, Undone
chapters.summary: Anders, POV, refuses to accept the confession; the family story is the only structure holding him up. He threatens to expose Daniel instead. Beatrix realizes the truth will never be free unless she gives it away herself. The beat: the last defender of a fortress no one else wants to garrison.

chapters.title: Time Already Running Out
chapters.summary: Daniel and Beatrix travel to see Elias. The prison visit is halting, wordless at first—fifteen years of postcards between them. Elias is weaker than either expected. Beatrix's POV; the beat is love against duty made flesh in a visiting-room chair.

chapters.title: Elias's Answer
chapters.summary: Elias's POV: he never wanted rescue; he wanted Beatrix to have the life he preserved for her. But dying, he admits he is tired of being the family's secret. He tells her the choice must be hers and must be public, or it means nothing. The beat: permission, hard-won and sorrowful.

chapters.title: The Confession
chapters.summary: Beatrix returns to Milton Flats and confesses publicly—at the reopened case, in front of Anders, the town, and the record. She names her father's crimes and her own. The law can no longer prosecute her fully, but the town must now live with the truth. Her POV; the beat is terror transfigured into freedom.

chapters.title: What Anders Carries
chapters.summary: Anders, POV, in the aftermath: stripped of the family story, he begins his own accounting, visiting their father's grave and finally speaking to Maren honestly. He does not forgive Beatrix yet, but he stops defending the lie. The beat: grief as the beginning of loyalty's honest form.

chapters.title: The Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Elias, dying, receives Beatrix in person; she reads him every postcard she ever wrote, and they burn the box together—delivered at last. Daniel stays at her side, no longer a stranger. Her POV; the beat is release, and the quiet cost of fifteen lost years.

chapters.title: The Weather of Milton Flats
chapters.summary: Months later, Beatrix's epilogue: Elias's funeral, small and honest, the family standing together under an ordinary sky. She writes one final postcard and mails it—to herself, at her own address, saying it plainly at last. The beat: a life no longer arranged around a question, but open like weather.
